title: The Bell in the Night
part: PART FOUR: THE NIGHT OF THE NORTH WIND

pages.text:
*The Owl Alley Sheet, No. 16. Today's news: the bell rang in the night.*

The sound did not start. It arrived.

One moment Haru was sleeping in the loft, her body warm under the futon. The next, a deep, booming crash shook the wooden frame of the sleeping room. It was not the wind. It was not the canal. It was a bell, struck with all the force a person could give, and it did not stop.

Haru sat up. Her heart beat in her ears, loud and hard. The shutters, which had been dark, now glowed with a faint, pulsing orange light. The shadows in the room stretched and bent like long, thin fingers.

Across the loft, Grandfather Tobei was already at the head of the ladder. He did not look up. He rubbed his bad shoulder, then dropped his hand to grab the rung. His face was pale in the orange light, but his voice was steady.

"Go, go, go," he said. "Do not wait for the lantern. The eyes are enough."

Haru was already moving. She did not think about what to wear. She did not think about her hair. She kicked off the futon, took his good arm, and helped him down the ladder one rung at a time, her bare feet slapping against the cold wooden rungs. The bell rang again, closer now, or maybe louder. The whole shop seemed to lean into the sound.
pages.image: Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in her rust-orange kimono with her hair coming loose, holds the arm of Grandfather Tobei, a thin old man with a white topknot in a blue-grey kimono, as they climb down a wooden ladder from a dark loft, the faint orange glow of a fire coming through the paper shutters behind them.

pages.text:
The alley was a river of noise.

The air smelled of wet wood and cold ash. People moved in a blur of dark kimono and bright panic. A woman carried a child wrapped in a thick blanket, her face tight with worry. A man ran past carrying a bucket filled with water, the liquid sloshing over his hands and dripping onto the frozen mud.

*Clack, clack, clack.*

The wooden geta hit the hard ground. It was the heartbeat of the chaos. Haru pushed through the crowd. Her breath came in short, sharp bursts.

She saw Father Sota. He was broad-shouldered and calm, carrying a heavy chest of wooden blocks on his back. Beside him, Kichi ran. His face was white. In one arm, he held a bundle of carving knives. In the other, he held a cat.

The cat meowed. It was a high, thin sound that cut right through the roar of the bell.

"Captain Daigoro!" a voice shouted from the far end of the alley.

Daigoro stood in the center of the street. He wore his leather hood, the black trim standing out against the night. He raised his long pole, the paper tassel at the top whipping in the wind.

"Stay back!" he bellowed, his voice ringing over the crowd. "Stay back and listen! Do not run toward the fire!"

Haru looked at the end of the alley. The darkness was not empty anymore. It was breathing.
pages.image: Captain Daigoro, a square man in a leather firefighter's coat and hood, stands in a narrow wooden alley at night, raising a long pole with a paper tassel, while Father Sota carries a wooden chest on his back and Kichi, a gangly boy in a moss-green coat, runs beside him holding knives and a cat.

pages.text:
Haru reached the bridge.

The wooden planks were cold under her feet. She looked across the canal, toward the bathhouse. The noise stopped for a second, and in that silence, she saw it.

It was not a mountain of flame. Not yet. It was a line.

A thin, red line ran along the base of the tall brick chimney. It glowed with a fierce, angry light. The wind, which had been silent for so long, suddenly spoke. It pushed the air across the canal, and with it, it pushed the smoke.

Haru watched, her hands trembling on the bridge railing, as a single spark leaped out of the ash door at the base of the furnace, which hung a little open, and rode the wind. It was a tiny, bright eye in the dark. It drifted over the water, over the stone wall, and landed on a pile of cherry-wood shavings that sat behind the furnace door.

The shavings did not catch slowly. They burst.

A whoosh of orange light erupted from the pile, licking up the side of the bathhouse wall. The wind caught the new flame and pulled it higher, stretching it into a long, thin tongue that pointed directly at the roof tiles. The sound of the fire was different from the bell. It was a hiss, a crack, a hungry roar.

Haru stepped back. Her hands were shaking so hard she had to clench them into fists.
pages.image: Haru in her rust-orange kimono watches from a wooden bridge at night with her hands clenched tight as a single bright spark drifts across a canal from a low wooden bathhouse with a tall brick chimney toward a heap of pale wood shavings that bursts into orange flame.

pages.text:
The door at the back of the bathhouse flew open.

Shin ran out, small and skinny, his face a mask of black soot and white skin. His eyes were huge and wide in the dirt. He held a bucket of water, his arms shaking with the effort of lifting it.

He ran to the pile of burning shavings. He did not look at the neighbors gathering in the street. He looked only at the flame.

He threw the water.

The liquid hit the fire and hissed into steam. But the wind was strong. It caught the vapor and the sparks and threw them back. The flame flared, doubling in size, leaping over the bucket Shin held.

Shin did not stop. He ran back to the well, filled the bucket again, and ran back. He threw the water again. The wind threw the fire back.

Hachi, the bathhouse owner, appeared from the shadows. His dark navy coat flapped behind him. He moved with surprising speed. He grabbed Shin by the collar of his soot-grey jacket and dragged him backward, away from the heat.

"Shin!" Hachi roared, his voice cracking. "Shin, come with me!"

Shin struggled, his feet skidding on the wet ground, but Hachi was stronger. He pulled the boy toward the street, his eyes fixed on the fire, but his body shielding the child.
pages.image: Hachi, a large man in a dark navy coat, drags a small, soot-covered boy named Shin away from a burning pile of wood shavings, the boy holding a bucket and struggling, while the orange glow of the fire illuminates their faces in the dark alley.

pages.text:
Haru stood frozen for one breath while the fire climbed past the shavings and licked the wall. Now it was on the roof, where the tiles glowed red, then orange, then white, turning the air into a thick black cloud that rolled over the alley and choked her lungs.

She looked down at her hands, still clenched tight, and then back at the fire, which looked as hungry as Kichi before breakfast.

Then she saw Okiku. The noodle stall was pulled up against the bathhouse wall, heavy with bowls and ingredients. Okiku stood in front of it, her face pale, her hands gripping the wooden handle so hard her knuckles were white. She could not move it. The weight was too much for one person.

Haru ran. She did not think about the danger, or the heat already kissing her face, only the heavy wooden wheels. She reached the cart and grabbed the handle behind Okiku.

"Push," Haru said. Her voice was steady.

Okiku pushed. Haru pulled. The wooden wheels groaned against the frozen ground, fighting the ice like a stubborn mule, and they moved the cart, inch by inch, away from the wall.

Behind them, the roof of the bathhouse gave way. A long sheet of orange fire rolled over the edge and hung in the air for a second, suspended by the wind, before dropping toward the tofu shop next door.
pages.image: Haru, in a rust-orange kimono, and Okiku, an older woman in a faded pink jacket, strain together to pull a heavy wooden cart away from a building wall, their faces strained with effort, while a massive sheet of orange fire rolls over the roof behind them.
